Does recursion amplify capability in the same way across very different fields?

Theory The Foundational Paper of the ARC Theory, within Recursive Dynamics: the foundation of Law I, the ARC Principle, a law under test

Michael Darius Eastwood

Independent Researcher, London, United Kingdom

The Foundational Paper of the ARC Theory, within Recursive Dynamics: the cross-domain foundation of Law I, the ARC Principle, and the formalism of the growth exponent that Law III, the ARC Ceiling, caps, each a law under test; it states the ARC Bound as the theory registration holds it, a ceiling of at most two for correctors of the system’s own class, whose point value two is a conjecture, and it bears on Law V, the ARC Embedding Law (added on 24 September 2026 and registered as a law on 15 October 2026 in version 1.103 of that registration, a law under test, the registered result on its placement limb given in Section 8; its mathematics in development), through the conditional prediction of Section 6.5, beside which it reports a pilot of the Eden Protocol. Abstract

I believe advanced AI is an existential risk unless values and correction are built into how it reasons; only proof will move the world. If control of a capable AI system were lost and could not be won back, what the system itself carries would decide what it does. This paper asks whether recursion amplifies capability in the same way across very different fields, so that a self-improving system’s growth could be predicted before it scales. Between 2024 and 2026, programmes in AI reasoning, quantum error correction, acoustic physics and consciousness science reported results that bear on recursive or recurrent processing, in different forms. We formalise the question with three axioms (separability, cumulative advantage, continuity) and a recursive composition operator. Under each case’s hypotheses, Cauchy’s functional equations give multiplicative composition a power law and additive composition an exponential; capped composition stays bounded. Inside the model the asymptotic exponent is derived, not fitted: α=1/(1−βL)\alpha = 1/(1-\beta_L) for coupling βL\beta_L; base potential and depth must interact multiplicatively; and a crossover depth R*=α/aR^* = \alpha/a, independent of base potential, separates approximately linear from compounding gains. Five structural properties follow, two on premises added to the axioms. The ARC Bound is stated as registered: the ceiling of Law III, the ARC Ceiling, a law under test, is at most two for same-class correctors, and the point value two is a conjecture. The evidence is graded: the AI exponent’s one interpretable fit is inconclusive, the time crystal is an analogy with no exponent measured, and the neuroscience mapping is structural. Thirteen falsification criteria and a cross-domain forward prediction are stated; a computational suite checks the closed forms but tests no real system. Each result holds inside its stated model.

Version 5.21 states Unit 83’s registered result, states the ARC Bound as the theory registration states it, grades the runs of March 2026, the alignment run and the time crystal as their sources and the corrections register now do, and moves the dated notes the body kept beside corrected text into Appendix B, which lists every version and correction, with its date.

1 Introduction

I believe advanced AI is an existential risk unless values and correction are built into how it reasons; only proof will move the world. If control of a capable AI system were lost and could not be won back, what the system itself carries would decide what it does. The programme’s position is that people keep oversight, containment and shutdown for as long as they physically can, and never give them up by choice; correction built into a system is the contingency for control lost against our will, not a reason to let go of it. If the way a recursive process combines its gains fixes how its capability grows with depth, then the scaling of a self-improving system could be predicted from a property measured before it scales: if you can measure the composition operator in a new system, you can predict its scaling function before measuring the full scaling curve (Section 3.2). On that reading, structural alignment (embedding values within the composition operator itself; the values are for international consensus, Section 6.5) is to be built while systems remain frozen and their scaling is predictable, and judged on whether it keeps a system useful as well as safe. This paper asks whether recursion amplifies capability in the same way across very different fields: is the pattern that separate research programmes have reported (Section 1.1) a coincidence, or are we observing different expressions of a single structural principle?

This paper belongs to the ARC Theory, the founding theory of Recursive Dynamics, the science of systems that improve themselves, which the author founded (the founding paper). The theory is carried by five laws, each a law under test: Law I, the ARC Principle, that usable capability is a power of recursive depth, with the exponent measured rather than assumed; Law II, the ARC Co-Scaling Law; Law III, the ARC Ceiling; and Laws IV and V, the ARC Persistence Law and the ARC Embedding Law, added on 24 September 2026, their mathematics in development. The laws and twenty-two propositions are registered on OSF (the theory registration), and the statement paper states the theory whole. The programme’s engineering hypothesis is the Eden Protocol, correction built into a system’s own reasoning, whose pilot Section 6.5 reports; its end goal is to learn, by registered tests, whether correction built into a self-improving system can keep pace with its capability, as the contingency for control lost against our will. This paper brings four fields together, AI reasoning, quantum error correction, acoustic physics and consciousness science, and assumes no reader knows the others: Section 1.1 says what each reported, and Appendix G places the paper among the laws.

We argue that the pattern reflects a principle, but not the one that might be expected. We do not claim that one equation fits all domains. We claim something more specific: that, for any recursive system that satisfies the axioms, a measurable property (its composition operator) determines its scaling function, and that five qualitative properties follow from the recursive architecture, two of them on premises added to the axioms (Theorem 4). The mathematical form differs across domains because the composition operator differs. The structural properties hold in every substrate whose recursion satisfies the axioms, because the axioms name no substrate.

Our contributions are:

  • A formalism. Three axioms, separability, cumulative advantage and continuity (Section 3.1), and the recursive composition operator ⊕\oplus, which characterises how incremental gains combine with accumulated capability (Definition 1), giving the generalised ARC Equation (2).

  • A classification. Under each case’s hypotheses, multiplicative ⊕\oplus yields power-law scaling (RαR^{\alpha}), additive ⊕\oplus yields exponential scaling (eαre^{\alpha r} in the added passes r=R−1r = R - 1), and bounded ⊕\oplus yields saturation (Theorem 1), each form stable within its own functional equation (Section 3.2).

  • The exponent derived, not fitted. Within the stated model, the asymptotic exponent is α=1/(1−βL)\alpha = 1/(1-\beta_L) (Theorem 2); no additive decomposition of capability is consistent with the axioms (Theorem 2a); and the crossover depth R*=α/aR^* = \alpha/a is independent of base potential (Theorem 3).

  • Five structural properties, threshold behaviour, recursive depth dependence, base quality dependence, multiplicative I×RI \times R interaction and regime boundaries, whose conjunction is the framework’s distinctive prediction (Theorem 4), and composition operator transitions within a single bounded system (Conjecture 5, supported in three computational systems and untested in physical experiments, not derivable from the three axioms).

  • The ARC Bound, stated as registered. The claim that the ceiling of Law III, the ARC Ceiling, is at most two for correctors of the system’s own class, which needs P6 and P20 and nothing else, with the point value two a conjecture; this paper’s own earlier form of it, the coupling at which the sustained exponent reaches two (βL=0.5\beta_L = 0.5, α=2\alpha = 2), is an early-framework conjecture that decides nothing registered (Section 6.4).

  • Graded evidence and tests. Evidence from four domains (Section 4), thirteen falsification criteria (Section 7), a cross-domain forward prediction (Section 6.1), a measurement protocol (Appendix E) and a computational validation suite checking the core mathematical relationships to machine precision (Appendix F).

The ARC Principle is Law I as the theory registration states it: usable capability is a power of recursive depth, with the exponent measured rather than assumed. The first four items are this paper’s framework for it, and the conjunction of the five properties of Theorem 4 is the framework’s own claim, tested by criterion F4; Law I takes its word through P1 alone, so no result on F4 refutes Law I. The power law is the form the framework derives for multiplicative composition, and the registration places the cross-domain claims beside Law I, as P9 and P18. The fifth item belongs to Law III, the ARC Ceiling, a law under test.

Section 1.1 sets out the four programmes and the question they raise, and Section 1.2 the ARC Equation and its generalisation. Section 2 places the work among related work, antecedents and the rival instrument. Section 3 gives the formalism: the axioms, the composition operator and Theorems 1 to 4. Section 4 reviews the evidence property by property, Section 5 explains the forms across domains, and Section 6 states the predictions and the ARC Bound as registered. Section 7 lists the falsification criteria, Section 8 says what the paper does and does not show, Section 9 states its limitations, and Section 10 concludes. Appendix A gives the proofs, Appendix B the version history and every correction, Appendix C the priority record, Appendix D the notation, Appendix E the measurement protocol, Appendix F the computational validation suite, and Appendix G the paper’s place in the ARC Theory.

1.1 The problem

Between August 2024 and February 2026, four research programmes reported the following results:

Google Quantum AI (results announced 9 December 2024; the team’s preprint public from 24 August 2024) demonstrated exponential suppression of the logical error rate below the surface-code threshold on the Willow processor, by a factor Λ=2.14±0.02\Lambda = 2.14 \pm 0.02 for each increase of two in code distance (Google Quantum AI and Collaborators 2024), a result graded here as convergent timing, not a prediction.

DeepSeek-AI (preprint January 2025; in Nature, September 2025) showed that “the reasoning abilities of LLMs can be incentivized through pure reinforcement learning (RL)”, with the emergence of reasoning patterns such as self-reflection and verification (Guo et al. 2025). Sharma and Chopra (2025) reported that sequential refinement, in which chains build on previous attempts, outperformed parallel self-consistency at matched compute in 95.6% of configurations, across five open-source models and three reasoning benchmarks. Their paper is dated before the experiment reported here, so it is the earlier demonstration of that advantage and not a confirmation of this work. The direction is also not settled: Gu et al. (2026), posted in April 2026, report the opposite result, parallel sampling outperforming sequential across three model families on mathematics and coding, attributing it to reduced exploration when a chain conditions on its own previous answers.

NYU Physics (February 2026) created a continuous classical time crystal with a pair of acoustically levitated beads: “Unless the particles have identical scattering properties, their wave-mediated interactions are nonreciprocal”, and pairs can use this nonreciprocity “to harvest energy from the wave to sustain steady-state oscillations despite viscous drag and the absence of periodic driving” (Morrell et al. 2026). The oscillation is a linearly stable limit cycle. In one experiment the antisymmetric mode’s coherence time is τ=(100±10)\tau = (100 \pm 10) s, about 6,700 cycles at 66.787 Hz, comparable to the 108 s recording, and the authors add: “Sustained oscillations persist for hours longer than the measurement window, which means that the true coherence time of the nonequilibrium steady state may be substantially larger.” Every recording the paper reports is of a steady state, and no growth exponent has been measured in this system.

The COGITATE Consortium (2025) found information about conscious content in visual, ventrotemporal and inferior frontal cortex, content-specific decoding in posterior regions generalising for about the duration of the stimulus (0.5 to 1.5 s) while in prefrontal regions its temporal generalisation was restricted to about 0.2 to 0.4 s (Cogitate Consortium et al. 2025). COGITATE tested two theories of consciousness, not a recursion depth, and its results challenge key tenets of both; this paper reads the sustained, content-specific posterior responses as structurally consistent with depth-dependent, feedback-driven processing, which COGITATE did not measure.

These programmes address different problems in different physical substrates. They report different things: exponential suppression of error in quantum error correction, a contested sequential advantage in AI reasoning, a sustained steady-state limit cycle in a classical time crystal, and no measured form in neuroscience. They are separate programmes in separate fields.

Yet, on this paper’s reading, they share a structural pattern: in each, recursive or recurrent processing (where the output of one cycle becomes the input for the next), operating on structured asymmetry, is what the reported gain or order depends on. Those programmes are cited for convergence and not for mechanism: whether any of their systems accumulates, meaning retains something from each pass whose contribution grows with depth, rather than merely conditioning on the previous pass, is untested in each case. The question this paper addresses is whether that pattern reflects a single underlying principle or mere coincidence.

1.2 The ARC Equation

We formalise the question as follows. For AI systems, the equation is U=I×Rα,α≤2,\begin{equation*} U = I \times R^{\alpha}, \quad \alpha \leq 2 , \end{equation*}(1) the ARC Equation (AI power-law form), with the ARC Bound, the registration’s claim that the ceiling of Law III, the ARC Ceiling, a law under test, is at most two for correctors of the system’s own class; Paper X supersedes this fixed-exponent framing as the operative safety criterion and re-scopes, without retracting, the equation and the bound (Section 6.4). Here α\alpha is the measured exponent (on today’s frozen models, one model’s fit and inconclusive; Section 4.3 prints its row whole). The two is not a property of the equation: it is the value Law III’s ceiling, 1/(1−γ)1/(1-\gamma), returns where the correction-leverage exponent γ\gamma is one half, a point value the registration conjectures and does not assert (Section 6.4). Law II, the ARC Co-Scaling Law, a law under test, is stated as the registration states it, βC>k\beta_C > k: correction has the asymptotic scaling advantage where its exponent exceeds the drift exponent, burden has it where the correction exponent is the smaller, and at equality coefficients, delay, backlog and saturation decide the outcome. In Paper X’s minimal model, with positive gain drift, βC>k\beta_C > k decides whether the misalignment fraction vanishes, and with level drift as well the condition is βC>max⁡(k,0)\beta_C > \max(k, 0).

Here UU denotes effective capability (the letter’s earlier senses in this programme are recorded in Appendix D.1), II denotes base potential (structured asymmetry; the notation register’s base intelligence, what the system could do before any self-improvement), RR denotes recursive depth, and α\alpha denotes the scaling exponent. Within the stated model this paper derives α\alpha rather than fitting it: the asymptotic exponent follows from the self-referential coupling βL\beta_L via α=1/(1−βL)\alpha = 1/(1-\beta_L). That the exponent is bounded by two is not a result of this model: it belongs to Law III, and Section 6.4 states it as the registration does, a claim on the correction-leverage exponent and not on the coupling. In the v5 cross-architecture experiment of Paper II, the one interpretable sequential fit, on Gemini 3 Flash, is inconclusive, with both point estimates below one (Section 4.3); the sequential advantage was observed only where both exponents could be estimated, and super-linear scaling (α>1\alpha > 1) was not. The original prediction of super-linear scaling for current models was not borne out (Section 5.1); the mathematics is unaffected, since it does not fix βL\beta_L, but the empirical AI scaling regime is weaker than originally predicted.

But this power-law form is itself a special case. Define the recursive composition operator ⊕\oplus, which characterises how incremental gains combine with accumulated capability. Under continuity and associativity, ⊕\oplus determines the system’s scaling function uniquely: U(R)=I×f⊕(R,βL),\begin{equation*} U(R) = I \times f_{\oplus}(R, \beta_L) , \end{equation*}(2) the generalised ARC Equation. Under the regularity and composition hypotheses of Theorem 1: multiplicative ⊕\oplus yields power-law scaling (RαR^{\alpha}), additive ⊕\oplus yields exponential scaling (eαre^{\alpha r} in the added passes r=R−1r = R - 1), and bounded ⊕\oplus yields saturation.

2 Related work, antecedents and the rival instrument

The formalism rests on mathematics far older than this programme, and much of its cross-domain evidence is other researchers’ work, beside the programme’s own experiment, comparisons and pilot (Sections 4.3, 6.1 and 6.5); this section states each debt in the source’s own terms and then weighs the nearest work.

Functional equations and their stability.

The classification of Theorem 1 rests on Cauchy’s functional equations (Cauchy 1821); that a function approximately satisfying one of them lies near an exact solution of the same equation is the stability theorem of Hyers and Ulam (Hyers 1941; Ulam 1960). The renormalisation-group parallel of Section 3.2 draws on Kadanoff’s scaling picture for Ising models near the critical point (Kadanoff 1966) and on Wilson’s renormalisation group (Wilson 1971).

The dimensional formula.

Section 6.4 sets out the earlier derivations of α=d/(d+1)\alpha = d/(d+1), a formula this paper does not claim (West et al. 1997, 2004; Banavar et al. 1999, 2010; Demetrius 2008; Demetrius and Tuszynski 2010; Zhao 2022; Bettencourt 2013); what it adds is an account of why those derivations converge.

The forms, conceded.

The relation α=1/(1−βL)\alpha = 1/(1-\beta_L) of Theorem 2 is the exponent of the elementary solution of the separable equation Axiom 2 states. The same structure, a stock that grows at a rate proportional to a power below one of itself, is the knowledge production function of Jones (1995), whose long-run growth rate carries the factor 1/(1−ϕ)1/(1-\phi); the expression 1/(1−βL)1/(1-\beta_L) is also the sum of a geometric series, familiar as the Keynes multiplier (Keynes 1936) and as Dyson resummation (Dyson 1949), as Paper X’s novelty ledger records of this paper. Axiom 2’s name, cumulative advantage, is the term of Price (1976). What this paper adds is not these forms but the axioms that select among them and their reading across domains.

The four programmes and their neighbours.

The programmes of Section 1.1 are cited for convergence, not mechanism. A photonic metamaterial analogue of a continuous time crystal (Liu et al. 2023) and a continuous space-time crystal state driven by nonreciprocal optical forces (Raskatla et al. 2024) have also been reported; recurrent processing as a basis of consciousness has its own literature (Lamme 2006; Zheng et al. 2025); and the scaling of test-time compute in language models has been studied directly (Snell et al. 2024; Zeng et al. 2025; Li et al. 2025).

The pipes premise, with its contest.

The premise that transport networks set the pace of biological growth is not this programme’s claim to defend; it is the premise of a leading account in quantitative biology, and a contested one. West, Brown and Enquist derived the allometric scaling laws of biology from the geometry of nutrient-distribution networks (West et al. 1997; one of the most cited papers in its field, with an OpenAlex citation count of 5,046 as of 12 August 2026, a single-source and index-dependent count). The exact exponent remains contested: White and Seymour report basal metabolic rate proportional to body mass to the two-thirds power rather than three-quarters (White and Seymour 2003), and Kozłowski and Konarzewski have twice asked whether the model is “mathematically correct and biologically relevant” (Kozłowski and Konarzewski 2004, 2005). This programme’s premise needs only the mechanism, that the delivery network sets the ceiling, and not any particular exponent; the dispute over the exponent’s value leaves it untouched, but the critics question the mechanism too, so the programme takes it as a premise, and its biological reading stands or falls with it.

The exception West’s own group found.

The escape from the pipe limit is also not this programme’s assertion; it is measured in the urban scaling literature by the same senior author. Bettencourt et al. (2007) report, in the paper’s own words (their β\beta is a city-scaling exponent, not this paper’s coupling βL\beta_L): “Quantities reflecting wealth creation and innovation have β≈1.2>1\beta\approx1.2>1 (increasing returns), whereas those accounting for infrastructure display β≈0.8<1\beta\approx0.8<1 (economies of scale).” Infrastructure, the literal pipes, scales sublinearly; information-mediated activity scales superlinearly. They state the contrast with biology directly: “we discuss how cities are similar to, and differ from, biological organisms, for which β<1\beta<1”. They derive “growth equations, which quantify the dramatic difference between growth fueled by innovation versus that driven by economies of scale” (spelling as in the original). And their closing inference names the consequence: “This difference suggests that, as population grows, major innovation cycles must be generated at a continually accelerating rate to sustain growth and avoid stagnation or collapse.” On this paper’s reading, that is the shape of the open problem this framework addresses: in the findings of West’s group, information-mediated growth escapes the throughput limit, and the only brake in their framework is external and must be applied again and again, faster and faster. No internal limit is derived. The replacement limit, a ceiling belonging to the growing system itself, is the gap.

The pipes argument at fixed throughput.

Everything that grows is fed through a channel, and for everything before software, fixing the channel fixes the growth. Starve a tumour’s blood supply and its growth is held back. Fix a chain reaction’s fuel and geometry and it stops. Exhaust an epidemic’s susceptible hosts and it burns out. Astrophysics has a named, quantitative constraint of the same kind: the Eddington limit, a luminosity ceiling where radiation pressure balances gravity, not a hard ceiling on accretion, since ultraluminous X-ray sources sit well above it (Bachetti et al. 2014). The claim here is a generalisation of limits physics already accepts, not a new species of assertion. Two hard cases are handled deliberately. Cosmic inflation is excluded by scope: it is expansion of space, not growth of a structure on a substrate, and it ended by field dynamics rather than by running out of anything. Evolution is the sharpest case and it fits: biological complexity increased for billions of years at roughly fixed solar throughput, which is growth on information at fixed pipes, and it is also glacial, and it has no internal corrector at all, since selection is external. On this framework, evolution would carry a measurable exponent far below the ceiling; that is a hypothesis about biology falling out of a framework built for software, stated without a criterion or a planned test, and it lies outside the theory registration’s scope, which places biological systems among those “for which the framework offers an analogy and no measurement”. The physicist’s form of the objection is Landauer’s: computation is physically implemented, so software has pipes too. The fixed-substrate clock is the answer and appears beside the claim: the regime under study holds the physical substrate fixed and asks what still grows, which is why exogenous speed-ups are excluded by definition. The functional form of capability growth in recursive depth remains an empirical question, and the registered analysis does not assume the family: under P1 the power law is compared with its registered rivals, “the logarithmic form, the exponential form, a saturating form, a broken or piecewise power law with one change of regime, and the shifted finite-window solution of this framework’s own growth equation”, and a declining outcome is admissible.

The rival instrument.

The nearest work to this programme’s question, and the right paper to weigh it against, is Engels et al. (2025), first posted 25 April 2025. It asks how oversight itself scales and answers quantitatively: oversight success is modelled as a game between capability-mismatched players whose oversight-specific Elo is a piecewise-linear function of general intelligence with two plateaus, and optimal numbers of oversight levels are derived for Nested Scalable Oversight, in which trusted models oversee stronger untrusted models that then become the trusted models at the next step. The instrument is the difference. Their variable is the capability gap between overseer and overseen, measured in Elo. This programme’s variable is the composition class of the corrector, measured through the corrector’s own scaling exponent. They also state the design condition in slope form: oversight improves with capability when the overseer’s game-specific Elo rises faster with general Elo than the overseen system’s (mG>mHm_G > m_H), and they recommend iterating an oversight design until it does. Their framework has no term for what the overseer is made of, and this paper’s formalism has none either. The programme’s separate prediction, outside this paper’s model, is that iterated same-class oversight, of which Nested Scalable Oversight is an instance, stays capped however many rungs are added, while a cross-class corrector is not held to that cap. The theory registration’s P6 states the cap for same-class correctors, at or below one half, as a conjecture on the correction-leverage exponent of Law III (the ARC Ceiling, a law under test), an exponent the registration keeps distinct from Law II’s βC\beta_C. That is where the two programmes could disagree about a measurable quantity, and this paper does not decide it.

Antecedents and near-misses, each with its differential.

On the question: Hutter asked directly whether intelligence can explode (Hutter 2012, arXiv, 28 February 2012), undertaking to separate speed from intelligence explosion and to consider possible bounds on intelligence, augmenting the analysis of Chalmers (2010); the question itself goes back to Good (1966). What that literature does not contain is a derived ceiling with an architecture dependence; growth exponents of the form used here are older, as this section has conceded. On impossibility: three 2025 arXiv papers argue for limits on alignment or its control (Yao 2025b, public by 13 June 2025, attested by arXiv and independently observed by the Internet Archive; Yao 2025a, 3 July 2025; and Ball et al. 2025, 9 July 2025). All three are worst-case and qualitative: measure zero, coNP-completeness, cryptographic hardness. Their measured object is verification of a fixed system, and it is closed within its own terms; this programme’s measured object is a different one, persistence of alignment as capability compounds under recursive amplification, and closure of the first does not settle the second. None reports an average-case scaling exponent or a rate. The third concludes that “safety cannot be achieved by designing filters external to the LLM internals (architecture and weights)” and argues that “an aligned AI system’s intelligence cannot be separated from its judgment”; that argument from filtering intractability is consistent with this programme’s architecture dependence, though it does not test it. On the mechanism: that anti-correlated estimates average better than independent ones is textbook variance reduction (antithetic variates); the mechanism is not the claim. The claim is that architecture determines whether anti-correlation is available at all, and that this caps a safety-relevant exponent. The nearest structural analogue is the quantum error-correction threshold theorem (Aharonov and Ben-Or 2008), which also converts a qualitative worry into a critical value; it concerns physical error rates in a fixed architecture, not a corrector’s scaling exponent, so it is a near-miss rather than an occupant, and the analogy was identified by this programme’s own search rather than by a referee. On feedback and stability, the general proposition that inadequate corrective gain relative to system gain causes instability has a long control-theory lineage (small-gain theorems; Zames 1966); those are gain conditions on interconnected systems, not a power-law exponent criterion on a corrector’s scaling with the capability of a recursively improving system. The nearest quantitative neighbour is Liu and Meng (2026), which recasts self-correction as a closed-loop control problem via a two-state Markov model and derives a directly measurable stability threshold, iterate only when the error-correction rate over the error-introduction rate exceeds Acc/(1−Acc)\mathrm{Acc}/(1-\mathrm{Acc}). The differential: theirs is a per-step rate threshold at a fixed capability level, deciding whether another iteration helps now; this programme’s criterion is a scaling relation across capability, deciding whether corrective strength keeps pace as the system improves. Theirs has no scaling exponent on the corrector and no capability-growth exponent, the two quantities the programme’s co-scaling criterion compares; the two models meet where growth stops, as Paper X shows. Smolin’s cosmological natural selection (Smolin 1992) is the antecedent for selection-shaped universes, and the programme’s own December-era notes cite it contemporaneously.

A programme hypothesis beyond the model.

Oversight arrangements that place a human in the loop, as amplification and reinforcement learning from human feedback do, are cross-class by construction, because the human corrector does not share the model’s substrate. The programme therefore hypothesises, beyond what this paper’s equations decide, that human-in-the-loop oversight shows a higher correction exponent than pure-model oversight, for a structural reason rather than a sentimental one. This is testable on existing data and does not require new systems.

3 The formalism

3.1 Three axioms

We begin with three axioms that define the recursive amplification systems this paper treats.

Axiom 1 (Separability). Effective capability decomposes as U=I×g(R)U = I \times g(R), where I>0I > 0 is base potential (structured asymmetry; the notation register’s base intelligence), R≥1R \geq 1 is recursive depth, and g(1)=1g(1) = 1 (at depth 1, capability equals base potential).

This axiom asserts that base quality and recursive depth contribute to capability through independent, multiplicative channels. A system with zero base potential (I=0I = 0) achieves zero capability regardless of recursive depth: recursion has nothing to amplify.

Axiom 2 (Cumulative advantage). The amplification factor grows according to accumulated amplification: dgdr=a⋅gβL\frac{dg}{dr} = a \cdot g^{\beta_L}, where the variable r=R−1r = R - 1 tallies the passes taken after the first, so that g=1g = 1 at r=0r = 0 restates Axiom 1’s g(1)=1g(1) = 1 in the added-recursion notation the proofs work in, a>0a > 0 is a rate constant and βL∈[0,1)\beta_L \in [0, 1) is the self-referential coupling parameter.

This axiom captures the essential feature of recursive processing: each step’s marginal amplification depends on accumulated amplification. When βL=0\beta_L = 0, steps are independent and amplification grows linearly. When βL>0\beta_L > 0, accumulated amplification accelerates future gains (super-linear scaling). The parameter βL\beta_L measures how much of accumulated context each new step can effectively leverage. Operating on the amplification factor gg rather than on absolute capability Q=I⋅gQ = I \cdot g preserves the separability asserted in Axiom 1: the amplification function depends only on recursive depth, not on base potential.

Axiom 3 (Continuity). The scaling function gg is continuous and monotonically non-decreasing in RR.

This is a regularity condition. It excludes pathological solutions and ensures measurability.

3.2 The composition operator

How does the gain from recursive step rr combine with accumulated capability QrQ_r? We formalise this as follows.

Definition 1 (Recursive composition operator). Let ⊕:ℝ+×ℝ+→ℝ+\oplus: \mathbb{R}^+ \times \mathbb{R}^+ \to \mathbb{R}^+ be the recursive composition operator, defined by Qr+1=Qr⊕δQrQ_{r+1} = Q_r \oplus \delta Q_r, where δQr\delta Q_r is the incremental gain at step rr. The operator ⊕\oplus characterises how incremental gains compose with accumulated capability.

The composition operator is the central mathematical object of this framework. It is what varies across domains and what determines the scaling function. It is also empirically measurable: observe how marginal gains at step rr relate to accumulated capability QrQ_r.

Theorem 1 (Classification of scaling functions). The algebraic properties of ⊕\oplus uniquely determine the scaling function f⊕(R)f_{\oplus}(R), under the premises each case names:

  1. Multiplicative composition (g(R1⋅R2)=g(R1)⋅g(R2)g(R_1 \cdot R_2) = g(R_1) \cdot g(R_2)): under Axioms 1 and 3, the unique continuous solution is g(R)=Rαg(R) = R^{\alpha} (power law).

  2. Additive composition (f(r1+r2)=f(r1)⋅f(r2)f(r_1 + r_2) = f(r_1) \cdot f(r_2) in the added passes r=R−1r = R - 1, with f(0)=1f(0) = 1): under Axioms 1 and 3, the unique continuous solution is f(r)=eαrf(r) = e^{\alpha r}, so that g(R)=eα(R−1)g(R) = e^{\alpha(R-1)} and g(1)=1g(1) = 1 (exponential).

  3. Bounded composition (Qr+1=min⁡(Qr+δQr,Qmax)Q_{r+1} = \min(Q_r + \delta Q_r,\; Q_{\max})), on the capped recurrence alone: f(R)f(R) is bounded by Qmax/IQ_{\max}/I and converges to a limit no greater than Qmax/IQ_{\max}/I, which it reaches only if the increments sum to at least the remaining gap, equality sufficing for attainment in the limit (saturation). Its ceiling is separable from base potential only if QmaxQ_{\max} is itself proportional to II.

Axiom 2 is not among the premises of cases (1) and (2).

Proof sketch. Cases (1) and (2) follow from the Cauchy functional equations. For (1): let h(x)=ln⁡g(ex)h(x) = \ln g(e^x); then h(x+y)=h(x)+h(y)h(x+y) = h(x) + h(y). Under continuity, h(x)=αxh(x) = \alpha x, giving g(R)=Rαg(R) = R^{\alpha}. For (2): ln⁡f\ln f satisfies ln⁡f(r1+r2)=ln⁡f(r1)+ln⁡f(r2)\ln f(r_1 + r_2) = \ln f(r_1) + \ln f(r_2), a Cauchy additive equation with solution ln⁡f(r)=αr\ln f(r) = \alpha r. Case (3) follows directly from the bound. Full proofs in Appendix A. ◻

What the classification settles is the behaviour of the three composition rules set out above. Two further continuous solutions of Cauchy’s equations remain, the linear form (f(R1+R2)=f(R1)+f(R2)f(R_1 + R_2) = f(R_1) + f(R_2)) and the logarithmic form (g(R1⋅R2)=g(R1)+g(R2)g(R_1 \cdot R_2) = g(R_1) + g(R_2)); neither compounds, and it is these that the parallel-voting data come close to, the logarithmic one being fitted outright in Appendix E. The premises of cases (1) and (2) are functional equations on the scaling function, and case (3)’s is a capped recurrence; that a given ⊕\oplus induces one of them is an assumption about the system, and the conclusions of cases (1) and (2) are Cauchy’s classical results (Cauchy 1821). The composition operator therefore classifies the scaling of every recursion whose scaling function satisfies one of Cauchy’s four equations or the capped recurrence of case (3); it is not a classifier of every recursion.

Frozen models versus recursive self-modification: two distinct regimes.

A critical application of this classification concerns the distinction between current AI systems and hypothetical self-modifying ones. Current frontier AI models are frozen during inference: when they generate extended reasoning chains, the underlying weights, and with them the composition rule, remain fixed (attention patterns still vary with the input). The composition operator ⊕\oplus does not change between steps. This architectural constraint confines such systems to multiplicative composition through a finite-dimensional parameter space, producing power-law fits with exponents below one, which Paper II names the physical regime, α<1\alpha < 1 (Section 5.1). Empirically, Paper II’s estimate of the exponent rests on one model, Gemini 3 Flash, and is inconclusive, with both sequential point estimates below one (Section 4.3 prints its row whole). Such a fit does not by itself place the model outside Axiom 2: α=1/(1−βL)\alpha = 1/(1-\beta_L) is the asymptotic exponent of the axiom’s solution, and over a finite window, below the crossover depth of Theorem 3, that solution can return a fitted exponent below one for a positive coupling.

The Cauchy classification reveals precisely why. In a frozen system the same fixed operator composes every reasoning step, and with α<1\alpha < 1 the resulting gains are real but diminishing. By contrast, a system capable of recursive self-modification, one that rewrites its own composition function ⊕\oplus during operation, would occupy a qualitatively different position in the classification. If step rr improves the operator used at step r+1r+1, the self-referential coupling βL\beta_L would, on this model, be positive and could rise, yielding α=1/(1−βL)>1\alpha = 1/(1-\beta_L) > 1. This transition does not require quantum hardware or additive composition; it requires only that the system can modify its own reasoning architecture during inference.

No current AI system achieves this. Earlier versions of this paper did predict super-linear scaling (α>1\alpha > 1) for current, frozen models (the original ARC Bound prediction, “testable within current model generations”, now kept in Appendix B.5), and that prediction was not borne out; the estimate of about 2.2 is retracted (Section 4.3). On the present reading, super-linear scaling belongs to a regime that does not yet exist. The practical consequence, previewed in Section 1, is that structural alignment is to be built while systems remain frozen and their scaling is predictable, and judged beside a measure of usefulness, as every safety measure is (Section 6.5). Once self-modification arrives, the composition operator becomes a moving target, and on this model a fixed external safeguard would fall behind a capability that compounds. Correction built into the operator is the contingency for control lost against our will; oversight, containment and shutdown stay in human hands for as long as they can be held. Guaranteed controllability after self-modification is not an established result of this programme.

Claim-status ladder.

Established mathematics: Cauchy’s equations constrain recursive scaling forms. Empirically grounded: current frontier models are frozen during inference; the Eden pilot found stakeholder-care scores, as its rubric scored them, raised by a prompt-level intervention in all five model runs that could be analysed, under paired tests, a pilot awaiting an independent, preregistered replication. The alignment run of March 2026 is not on this rung: it cannot decide whether alignment scales with depth (Section 6.5).

Strong theoretical inference: a genuinely self-modifying system that rewrites its own composition operator during operation could enter an α>1\alpha > 1 regime, and alignment would then need to be structurally load-bearing before that transition.

Conjectural extrapolation: set out at the close of the paper (Section 10).

The six hidden assumptions.

Every classification theorem rests on assumptions. Theorem 1 assumes six things. Each assumption, when violated, produces a specific physical refinement rather than a contradiction:

Table 1. The six hidden assumptions of Theorem 1.
# Assumption When violated Physical example
1 Continuity Log-periodic oscillations Discrete lattice systems, fractal networks
2 Real-valued Interference and phase Quantum amplitudes, wave mechanics
3 Exact equation Approximate solutions cluster near exact Hyers-Ulam stability (Hyers 1941; Ulam 1960)
4 Single operator Crossover scaling, regime transitions Phase transitions (cf. Conjecture 5)
5 Scalar composition Logarithmic corrections Upper critical dimension
6 Time-independence Dynamic traversal of solution space Adaptive systems, machine learning

Assumption 3 is particularly significant for the framework’s applicability. The Hyers-Ulam stability theorem (Hyers 1941; Ulam 1960) proves that any function approximately satisfying one of Cauchy’s functional equations must lie close to an exact solution of that same equation. Formally, for the additive equation, if |f(x+y)−f(x)−f(y)|≤ε|f(x + y) - f(x) - f(y)| \leq \varepsilon for all x,yx, y, there is an exact additive gg with |f(x)−g(x)|≤ε|f(x) - g(x)| \leq \varepsilon (Hyers 1941); for the exponential equation, and so for the multiplicative one by a change of variables, the result is superstability: a real function on a vector space with |f(x+y)−f(x)f(y)|≤ε|f(x + y) - f(x) f(y)| \leq \varepsilon for all x,yx, y is either bounded or an exact solution (Baker et al. 1979). Real systems never satisfy the axioms exactly: biological networks are noisy, AI reasoning chains have variable quality, quantum error correction operates with imperfect gates. Within each equation, the corresponding form is therefore stable under perturbation. The earlier phrasing that made the three forms “stable attractors in function space” is withdrawn, because a function that satisfies none of the equations is not drawn toward any of them; the stability is per-equation, not a partition of function space. Whether power laws, exponentials, or logarithmic forms are empirically ubiquitous in nature is a separate question about how often systems approximately satisfy one of these equations in the first place, and Hyers-Ulam does not by itself settle it.

Assumption 4 is addressed directly by Conjecture 5 (Section 5.5): bounded systems can transition between composition operators as recursive depth increases, which could explain why different studies of the same system can observe different scaling regimes.

Structural implication: per-equation stability.

Combining Theorem 1 (Cauchy 1821), the Hyers-Ulam stability theorem (Hyers 1941), and Theorem 2 (α=1/(1−βL)\alpha = 1/(1-\beta_L)): once a system is known to approximately satisfy one of Cauchy’s equations, its scaling form is not a free parameter to be fitted or evolved. It is mathematically compelled by the composition operator, and within the power-law form the exponent is compelled by the self-referential coupling βL\beta_L. Each of the recognised scaling forms is per-equation stable: a small perturbation of an exact solution stays near an exact solution of the same equation (Hyers 1941; Baker et al. 1979). The distinction matters: ‘Why is this system’s exponent 2?’ has two kinds of answer. The mechanistic answer describes the coupling. The mathematical answer says: no other value is possible for this composition operator with this coupling strength.

This has a crucial implication: if you can measure ⊕\oplus in a new system, you can predict its scaling function before measuring the full scaling curve. This is the framework’s strongest cross-domain prediction (Section 6.1).

Critical distinction: Cauchy constrains the form, not the exponent.

A persistent misreading of the Cauchy classification is that it predicts a ceiling on recursive scaling. It does not. Cauchy’s functional equations determine that multiplicative composition must produce power-law scaling (g(R)=Rαg(R) = R^\alpha). They say nothing about the value of α\alpha. That value is set by the Bernoulli ODE (α=1/(1−βL)\alpha = 1/(1-\beta_L)), and as βL→1\beta_L \to 1, α→∞\alpha \to \infty. There is no upper bound internal to the mathematics.

The following table makes the relationship explicit:

Table 2. The exponent α=1/(1−βL)\alpha = 1/(1-\beta_L) at values of the self-referential coupling βL\beta_L.
βL\beta_L (self-referential coupling) α=1/(1−βL)\alpha = 1/(1-\beta_L) Regime
0 1 Linear (no self-reference)
0.5 2 Quadratic
0.75 4 Quartic
0.9 10 Strongly super-linear
0.99 100 Explosive
→1\to 1 →∞\to \infty Unbounded

On this model, a system that modifies its own composition operator changes the scaling exponent itself; the passage from bounded to unbounded α\alpha is not a smooth acceleration within one operator. This has a structural parallel in the renormalisation group in physics (Wilson 1971), where relevant operators grow under RG flow and irrelevant operators shrink. At a critical fixed point, the scaling exponent is determined by the system’s universality class (its dimensionality and symmetry). But if a system could change its own universality class during the flow, the fixed-point structure would collapse and the system would exhibit unbounded scaling until it settled into a new class. As an analogy, not a derivation: a self-modifying AI system would resemble a physical system that rewrites its own Hamiltonian, escaping the fixed-point constraints that a fixed composition operator imposes.

If there is a ‘quadratic limit’ (α≤2\alpha \leq 2), it is not a Cauchy prediction. The value two comes from the pacing derivation of Law III, the ARC Ceiling, a law under test, at γ=1/2\gamma = 1/2 (Section 6.4; correction 9). The count of O(N2)O(N^2) pairwise attention pathways in a fixed transformer is a heuristic for why frozen architectures fall below it and proves nothing about capability (corrections 2 and 4). A self-modifying system that expands its own representational capacity at each step would not face that count, and the mathematics sets no upper bound on α\alpha: the Cauchy framework does not forbid an exponent above two, and it does not predict one.

3.3 The βL\beta_L-derivation

For systems with multiplicative composition, the exponent α\alpha is not a free parameter. It is derived from the coupling constant βL\beta_L.

Theorem 2 (The scaling exponent). Under Axiom 2, the power-law exponent is α=11−βL.\begin{equation*} \alpha = \frac{1}{1 - \beta_L} . \end{equation*}(3)

Proof. Separating variables in dg/dr=agβLdg/dr = a g^{\beta_L}: ∫g−βLdg=∫adr⇒g1−βL1−βL=ar+C.\begin{equation*} \int g^{-\beta_L}\, dg = \int a\, dr \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \frac{g^{1-\beta_L}}{1-\beta_L} = ar + C . \end{equation*}(4) With initial condition g(0)=1g(0) = 1: C=1/(1−βL)C = 1/(1-\beta_L). In the clock Axiom 2 declares, r=R−1r = R - 1: g(r)=[1+(1−βL)ar]1/(1−βL),r≥0,\begin{equation*} g(r) = \left[ 1 + (1-\beta_L)ar \right]^{1/(1-\beta_L)}, \qquad r \geq 0 , \end{equation*}(5) equivalently g(R)=[1+(1−βL)a(R−1)]1/(1−βL)g(R) = \left[ 1 + (1-\beta_L)a(R-1) \right]^{1/(1-\beta_L)} for R≥1R \geq 1. In the deep recursion limit (R≫R*R \gg R^*, defined below): g(R)≈[(1−βL)aR]1/(1−βL)∝R1/(1−βL).\begin{equation*} g(R) \approx \left[ (1-\beta_L)aR \right]^{1/(1-\beta_L)} \propto R^{1/(1-\beta_L)} . \end{equation*}(6) Therefore α=1/(1−βL)\alpha = 1/(1-\beta_L). ◻

This transforms α\alpha from a fitted constant into a derived quantity. The derivation makes a specific, testable prediction: measure βL\beta_L independently (by observing how marginal gains depend on accumulated capability), compute the predicted α\alpha, and compare with the observed α\alpha. If the relationship fails, Axiom 2 does not describe that system, whether or not the power-law form holds empirically.

Computational check. As a check on the numerics (the identity itself is proved above), the relationship was tested against 30 exact Bernoulli ODE solutions with βL\beta_L values spanning 0.05 to 0.92. The procedure measures βL\beta_L blindly from marginal gains (dg/dRdg/dR vs gg in log-log space, estimated by finite differences of the noiseless closed-form solutions), predicts α\alpha, and compares against the true value; Section 9 reports that numerical derivatives of noisy data bias this estimate. Result: R2=1.00000000R^2 = 1.00000000 (eight decimal places), regression slope =1.000102= 1.000102, mean absolute prediction error =0.002%= 0.002\%. The code is listed under Code and data, after the conclusion.

The multiplicative structure is necessary.

The separable form U=I×f(R,βL)U = I \times f(R, \beta_L) is Axiom 1’s assumption. Theorem 2a makes explicit what that assumption excludes: once Axiom 1 holds and amplification is not trivial, no additive decomposition of capability is possible.

Theorem 2a (Non-additivity). Under Axioms 1 to 3 with βL∈(0,1)\beta_L \in (0, 1), the solution U(I,R)U(I, R) cannot be decomposed as U=f(I)+h(R)U = f(I) + h(R) for any functions ff and hh. The multiplicative interaction is essential.

Proof. Suppose U=f(I)+h(r)U = f(I) + h(r), with depth counted in added passes, r=R−1r = R - 1. By Axiom 1: U=I×g(r)U = I \times g(r) with g(0)=1g(0) = 1. At r=0r = 0 (R=1R = 1): f(I)+h(0)=If(I) + h(0) = I, so f(I)=I−h(0)f(I) = I - h(0). Substituting: I×g(r)=I+[h(r)−h(0)]I \times g(r) = I + [h(r) - h(0)], giving g(r)=1+[h(r)−h(0)]/Ig(r) = 1 + [h(r) - h(0)]/I. Since gg depends only on depth (Axiom 1), but the right side depends on II, we require h(r)=h(0)h(r) = h(0) for all rr, giving g(r)=1g(r) = 1 (no amplification). But Axiom 2 with βL>0\beta_L > 0 guarantees dg/dr=a⋅gβL=a>0dg/dr = a \cdot g^{\beta_L} = a > 0 at r=0r = 0, so gg is non-constant. Contradiction. ◻

This result has a concrete interpretation. A recursive system with zero base quality (I=0I = 0) produces zero capability regardless of depth, and a system at zero added passes (r=0r = 0, the first pass) produces only its base potential, unamplified. Complexity emerges from the interaction between structured input and recursive processing (neither alone is sufficient).

βL\beta_L (coupling) α\alpha (exponent) Interpretation

0.25 1.33 Weak coupling →\to mild super-linear
0.50 2.00 Moderate coupling →\to quadratic (the ARC Bound’s point value)

Note: The ARC Bound (Section 6.4) is registered as a ceiling of at most two for correctors of the system’s own class; this paper’s own earlier form of it, that a same-class sequential system cannot sustain βL>0.5\beta_L > 0.5 (α>2\alpha > 2), is a conjecture that decides nothing registered. The row with βL=0.67\beta_L = 0.67 shows the mathematical relationship for completeness; whether physical systems can access this regime is an open empirical question.

3.4 The scaling crossover R*R^*

The full solution to the βL\beta_L-dynamics equation is not a pure power law. It contains a transition.

Theorem 3 (The scaling crossover). In the clock Axiom 2 declares (r=R−1r = R - 1), the full solution g(r)=[1+(1−βL)ar]1/(1−βL)g(r) = \left[ 1 + (1-\beta_L)ar \right]^{1/(1-\beta_L)} exhibits three regimes:

  1. r≪R*r \ll R^*: g≈1+ar\;g \approx 1 + ar  (approximately linear amplification);

  2. r≫R*r \gg R^*: g∝Rα\;g \propto R^{\alpha}  (compounding dominates; power-law scaling);

  3. crossover at R*=αa\;R^* = \dfrac{\alpha}{a}, counted in added passes; counted from the first pass, the same depth is 1+α/a1 + \alpha/a.

R*R^* is the crossover depth: the recursive depth at which compounding overtakes linear gains. Below R*R^*, additional recursion provides approximately constant marginal benefit. Above R*R^*, returns compound and capability grows super-linearly.

Critically, R*R^* is a derived quantity. It depends on measurable parameters (α\alpha and aa) and is not a free parameter to be fitted. This provides an independent consistency check: measure α\alpha and aa separately, compute the predicted R*R^*, and verify that the observed crossover matches. Since R*R^* depends only on the scaling exponent and rate constant (not on base potential II), the crossover depth is a property of the recursive architecture itself, not of the input quality.

The existence of R*R^* is, to this programme’s knowledge, absent in this form from other scaling frameworks: crossover scales do turn up elsewhere (logistic growth, renormalisation-group crossovers), but what is predicted here is a crossover sited at R*=α/aR^* = \alpha/a, pinned by two parameters each of which can be measured on its own (a literature search of 12 August 2026, cross-checked against two years of repository reports; negative findings have the status of not-found-by-that-search, never does-not-exist). It distinguishes recursive amplification from simple redundancy: redundant systems show uniform (typically logarithmic) improvement with repetition; recursive systems show a qualitative transition at a specific, predictable depth.

3.5 Five derived properties

We now prove that any system satisfying Axioms 1 to 3 with βL>0\beta_L > 0 exhibits five structural properties, two of them on premises Theorem 4 names.

Theorem 4 (Universal structural properties). Let a recursive system satisfy Axioms 1 to 3 with βL>0\beta_L > 0. It exhibits the five properties below, each on the premises named with it:

  1. Threshold behaviour (Axioms 1 to 3, through Theorem 3). There exists a crossover depth R*R^* below which base capability dominates and above which recursive gains dominate. This follows from Theorem 3: the transition from U≈IU \approx I to U∝RαU \propto R^{\alpha} is a qualitative regime change.

  2. Recursive depth dependence (Axioms 1 and 2). Capability is a strictly increasing function of depth, and convex at every depth: differentiating Axiom 2 gives d2g/dr2=a2βLg2βL−1d^{2}g/dr^{2} = a^{2}\beta_L g^{2\beta_L-1}, which is strictly positive for a>0a > 0 and βL>0\beta_L > 0; R*R^* marks where compounding becomes numerically dominant, not where curvature begins.

  3. Base quality dependence (Axiom 1 alone). UU is proportional to II: capability is zero when I=0I = 0. This follows directly from Axiom 1: U=I×g(R)U = I \times g(R).

  4. Multiplicative I×RI \times R interaction. Doubling II doubles UU at any RR (Axiom 1 alone). Doubling RR multiplies UU by 2α2^{\alpha} at any II exactly in the pure-power case, where a=αa = \alpha, and asymptotically otherwise; under bounded composition the doubling law does not hold. The effects compose multiplicatively. This follows from the separable form U=I×g(R)U = I \times g(R).

  5. Regime boundaries (an added premise: finite resources and external error mechanisms). Physical systems have finite energy, introducing external error mechanisms that create ceilings. The pure power-law describes a regime between R*R^* and the saturation depth RmaxR_{\max} beyond which external factors dominate.

Remark 1. At βL=0\beta_L = 0 amplification runs linear. The best fit Paper II reports for a frozen model is one model’s and inconclusive (Section 4.3 prints its row whole), with both sequential point estimates below one; a power law with such an exponent is concave, but over a finite window the solution of Axiom 2, convex at every depth for βL>0\beta_L > 0, can return such a fit, so convexity reports nothing measured about the systems in use today. Property 5’s regime boundaries are visible in quantum error correction, where rare correlated error events set a floor near 10−1010^{-10} in high-distance repetition codes (Google Quantum AI and Collaborators 2024), and in AI, where accuracy ceilings appear at extreme reasoning depths. A time crystal’s oscillation is sustained at bounded amplitude on a stable limit cycle (Section 1.1); no growth toward it has been recorded, so it shows a bound, not a regime boundary in depth.

These five properties constitute this paper’s framework claim, the qualitative core of its account of Law I, the ARC Principle, a law under test; their conjunction is tested by criterion F4, and no result on F4 refutes Law I as registered (Section 1). The quantitative functional form (power-law, exponential, saturating) is domain-specific and determined by the composition operator. But the five structural properties follow from the axioms and the premises Theorem 4 names for each, and their conjunction is the framework’s distinctive prediction.

The five properties are individually common in physical systems. Threshold behaviour is ubiquitous. Depth dependence appears in many iterative processes. What is not common is the conjunction of all five in a single system. The framework predicts that all five co-occur whenever the three axioms and the premises Theorem 4 names are satisfied. A system with four of the five properties but not the fifth would show that it does not satisfy them, and would refute the framework’s claim for any system it was said to cover.

4 Evidence

We present evidence organised around the five derived properties, not by domain. For each property, we show how it manifests across systems. Evidence strength is classified as: Quantitative (a parameter of this framework measured in the system itself), Analogy (a quantity measured in another field, such as quantum error correction’s Λ\Lambda, read through this framework’s composition classes; the source does not test the framework, and the reading is this paper’s), Structural (qualitative mapping without quantitative α\alpha), or Consistent (does not contradict but was not designed to test ARC).

4.2 Property-by-property evidence

Property 1: threshold behaviour.

Quantum: The surface code threshold pthr≈1%p_{\text{thr}} \approx 1\% is a sharp phase boundary. Above it (p>pthrp > p_{\text{thr}}), a larger code distance makes performance worse. Below it (p<pthrp < p_{\text{thr}}), each increase of two in code distance suppresses the logical error rate by a further factor, so the suppression is exponential in distance. This is the most precisely measured threshold in the evidence base: Google varied physical error rates through controlled error injection and observed the threshold directly (Google Quantum AI and Collaborators 2024).

Physics: The time crystal’s exceptional point (where two eigenvalues of the stability matrix coalesce) marks, on this paper’s reading, the transition from symmetric (bounded) to antisymmetric (compounding) dynamics. Below threshold: active oscillator. At threshold: exceptional point. Above threshold: time crystal (Morrell et al. 2026). The exceptional point is computed from the source’s model; none is measured. Here and throughout this section, the time crystal is a consistency check and a cross-domain analogy, not a test of the framework, and no study of it is registered.

AI: The sequential-vs-parallel distinction functions as a threshold. Sequential processing (output→\toinput feedback) achieves αseq>αpar\alpha_{\text{seq}} > \alpha_{\text{par}} in the v5 experiment wherever both exponents could be estimated, among the five frontier models measured on both arms, capability and alignment (Paper II). The threshold is structural: it is the presence or absence of the feedback loop, not a continuous parameter (Sharma and Chopra 2025).

Property 2: recursive depth dependence.

Quantum: Logical error rate decreases as εd∝Λ−(d+1)/2\varepsilon_d \propto \Lambda^{-(d+1)/2} with code distance dd. Each increase of two in dd enlarges the code’s lattice of physical qubits, and the suppression factor Λ\Lambda applies for each such step (Google Quantum AI and Collaborators 2024); the paper reads code distance as its depth variable by analogy, since the surface code is not a concatenated, recursive code.

AI: Sharma and Chopra (2025) tested seven voting methods for aggregating sequential chain outputs. Methods favouring later reasoning steps (inverse-entropy weighting) achieved optimal performance in 97% of configurations; methods favouring earlier steps achieved optimality in only 17%. This 80-percentage-point gap indicates that later recursive steps carry systematically more information about the correct answer, consistent with capability that compounds with depth (Sharma and Chopra 2025).

Physics: In the source’s linear stability analysis the antisymmetric (breathing) mode grows when the pair lies in its active region, “leading to spontaneous breathing-mode oscillations” (Morrell et al. 2026). Every recording is of a steady state, so that growth has not been observed and no dependence on cycle count has been measured.

Property 3: base quality dependence.

Quantum: Λ=pthr/p\Lambda = p_{\text{thr}}/p depends directly on physical qubit quality (pp). Worse qubits (pp closer to pthrp_{\text{thr}}) give Λ→1\Lambda \to 1 and error correction barely helps. Active leakage removal (DQLR), which maintains qubit quality during operation, improved Λ\Lambda by 35% at distance 5 (Google Quantum AI and Collaborators 2024).

Physics: In the source’s model the pair is active only when the beads differ in size: unless the particles have identical scattering properties their interactions are nonreciprocal, and “The active region vanishes for particles of the same size (a1=a2a_1 = a_2), whose interactions are reciprocal” (Morrell et al. 2026). The framework reads this as an instance of its zero-factor property, a correspondence of structure and not a test.

AI: Single-pass accuracy without reasoning chains determines base capability II. On this framework, a model with higher II benefits more from sequential reasoning at any depth; no work cited here measures that comparison.

Property 4: multiplicative I×RI \times R interaction.

Quantum: εd=(p/pthr)(d+1)/2=Λ−(d+1)/2\varepsilon_d = (p/p_{\text{thr}})^{(d+1)/2} = \Lambda^{-(d+1)/2}. The base quality factor Λ\Lambda and the depth factor (d+1)/2(d+1)/2 interact multiplicatively in log-space: ln⁡εd=−d+12ln⁡Λ\ln \varepsilon_d = -\frac{d+1}{2} \ln \Lambda. Improving Λ\Lambda by a factor has the same proportional effect at any depth (Google Quantum AI and Collaborators 2024).

AI: In the ARC equation U=I×RαU = I \times R^{\alpha}, base capability and recursive depth are separated multiplicatively by construction (Axiom 1). With one base model, Snell et al. (2024) found that “the effectiveness of different approaches to scaling test-time compute critically varies depending on the difficulty of the prompt”; they did not measure how that benefit varies with the base model’s quality, so a benefit that grows with base quality is this paper’s reading, untested.

Property 5: regime boundaries.

Physics: The time crystal’s oscillation is sustained at bounded amplitude on a linearly stable limit cycle: in the source, higher-order damping can stabilise the growing mode, which then settles into steady-state oscillation (Morrell et al. 2026). Its measured coherence time (Section 1.1) is a property of that steady state, not a ceiling and not a time taken to reach it.

Quantum: In high-distance repetition codes, correlated error bursts create an error floor at approximately 10−1010^{-10} for code distances d≥15d \geq 15, preventing the exponential from continuing indefinitely (Google Quantum AI and Collaborators 2024).

AI: Zeng et al. (2025) found that longer reasoning chains do not consistently improve performance; correct solutions were often shorter than incorrect ones. Longer chains carry more self-revisions, which often degraded performance, and in some models accuracy rose in early revisions and then oscillated. The sequential advantage has boundary conditions (Zeng et al. 2025).

4.3 Contradictory evidence

Several studies challenge the framework’s AI predictions:

Zeng et al. (2025, arXiv:2502.12215) found that for DeepSeek R1, longer chains do not consistently enhance accuracy. Li et al. (2025, arXiv:2502.14382) found that hybrid parallel-sequential approaches outperform pure sequential on code generation. Sharma and Chopra’s (2025) own ablation showed parallel approaches achieve greater semantic diversity on creative tasks while sequential achieves greater lexical diversity, suggesting the sequential advantage applies most strongly to convergent tasks requiring iterative error correction (Sharma and Chopra 2025; Zeng et al. 2025; Li et al. 2025).

These results refine, rather than refute, the hypothesis. The sequential advantage appears to have boundary conditions: it holds within task-appropriate depth ranges, for convergent problems, and breaks down at extreme depths or for divergent tasks. Gu et al. (2026) report the opposite direction, parallel sampling outperforming sequential across three model families on mathematics and coding (Section 1.1), so the direction itself is contested.

The capability runs of March 2026.

The v5 experiment of Paper II tested six frontier models on 30 problems with bootstrap confidence intervals; five carried the capability arm, Grok 4.1 Fast, DeepSeek R1, Gemini 3 Flash, GPT-5.4 and Groq Qwen3, and Claude Opus 4.6 was measured only in the alignment arm. The five capability runs wrote their records between 11 March 2026 at 15:08 UTC and 12 March 2026 at 04:17 UTC, by the times their own code wrote into each result, and their code and results were first public by GitHub push on 16 March 2026. They are precursor evidence in the theory registration’s sense: they came before it, and they decide no proposition it registers; their two arms were not matched in compute. One sequential fit is interpretable, Gemini 3 Flash’s, and it is inconclusive: an endpoint estimate of 0.59 with a bootstrap 95 per cent interval of minus 1.3 to 2.9, and a regression estimate of 0.49 with a standard error of 0.20 and a coefficient of determination of 0.86, beside a parallel exponent of 0.31 by endpoint estimate. Paper II classifies the other four runs as near ceiling (Grok 4.1 Fast and DeepSeek R1), a step function (GPT-5.4) and a floor (Groq Qwen3), with no interpretable sequential exponent. It grades the sequential advantage as observed, “Wherever both exponents could be estimated: Gemini 3 Flash; DeepSeek R1, unreliably”, with no parallel exponent for Grok 4.1 Fast, and Gu et al. (2026) report the opposite direction. Neither super-linear scaling (α>1\alpha > 1) nor a single exponent across architectures was observed. The update of March 2026 that this section printed, with its table of that month’s estimates, stands in Appendix B.5.

The earlier estimates.

The author’s earlier α\alpha estimates (α≈1.34\alpha \approx 1.34 from n=2n=2 data points; α≈2.2\alpha \approx 2.2 from n=12n=12, 95% CI: 1.5 to 3.0) were preliminary. The later, about 2.2 from twelve problems on one model, is retracted; Paper II gives the reasons for its inflation as twelve problems, one model and a compressed dynamic range. The v5 best fit, Gemini 3 Flash’s (above), is what survived it, one model’s fit and inconclusive, not a correction of the same measurement. No α\alpha has been measured in time crystals. The COGITATE mapping is structural, not quantitative. The neuroscience term ‘recurrent’ and the computational term ‘recursive’ are related but not identical.

5 The composition operator across domains

The composition operator ⊕\oplus is not merely a classification tool. It explains why different domains exhibit different scaling functions.

5.1 AI: multiplicative composition

In chain-of-thought reasoning, each step builds hierarchically on accumulated insight. Step r+1r+1 does not merely add new information; it restructures the problem representation using everything accumulated through step rr. This is multiplicative composition: the gain at each step depends on the quality of the accumulated representation, less than proportionally (were it strictly proportional, growth would be exponential).

The βL\beta_L-dynamics equation dg/dr=agβLdg/dr = ag^{\beta_L} models this directly. If βL≈0.5\beta_L \approx 0.5 (moderate coupling), Theorem 2 gives α≈2\alpha \approx 2; the measured value is reported below.

Two derivations reach that value and they are not the same derivation, which this paper now states rather than leaves to be noticed. Theorem 2 gives the exponent the coupling sustains, α=1/(1−βL)\alpha = 1/(1 - \beta_L), where βL\beta_L is the leverage fraction of the recursive step. The ceiling is that of Law III, the ARC Ceiling, a law under test, αcrit=1/(1−γ)\alpha_{\text{crit}} = 1/(1 - \gamma), and it comes from the correction shortfall rather than from the coupling, where γ\gamma is the correction-leverage exponent (the registration’s letter, written χ\chi in the notation register). Both return two when their exponent is one half; in general they agree exactly where βL=γ\beta_L = \gamma on the same system, which is an open question and is preregistered by timestamp as one (first anchored on 12 August 2026; Appendix C): a drafted study, AG, estimates the coupling and the correction exponent on one and the same system and tests whether the growth exponent the leverage fraction sustains respects the ceiling the correction exponent sets (βL≤γ\beta_L \leq \gamma), and discloses in advance the precision that test needs. Written in the coupling, the stability condition α≤αcrit\alpha \leq \alpha_{\text{crit}} reads βL≤γ\beta_L \leq \gamma, which says that a system stays correctable exactly while the leverage it takes per step does not outrun the capacity it has to correct what that leverage costs, under the conditions the registration states for Law III (Section 6.4).

The coupling of today’s systems.

The original prediction that optimised language models with explicit self-correction would converge toward α≈2\alpha \approx 2 (βL≈0.5\beta_L \approx 0.5), testable within current model generations, was not borne out; it and its version 3.1 update stand in Appendix B.5. Paper II reads a sequential exponent below one as the physical regime, α<1\alpha < 1, and its one interpretable fit, Gemini 3 Flash’s, is inconclusive, with both point estimates below one (Section 4.3). Read through α=1/(1−βL)\alpha = 1/(1-\beta_L) alone, such an exponent would ask for a coupling below zero, outside Axiom 2’s range; but that relation gives the asymptotic exponent, and over a finite window the axiom’s solution can return a fitted exponent below one for a positive coupling (Section 3.2). Whether any deployed system lies inside the regime that Theorem 2 and Laws II and III, each a law under test, govern is therefore unmeasured: no coupling has been estimated independently on any system, and that comparison is what P5 registers (Section 6.2).

5.2 Quantum: additive composition

In surface code quantum error correction, each increase of two in code distance multiplies the suppression of the logical error rate by the same factor Λ\Lambda. The surface code is not concatenated: a larger distance enlarges one lattice, and syndrome extraction repeats in time, cycle by cycle, not distance by distance; the paper reads code distance as its depth variable by analogy. The gains accumulate additively (in code distance) while composing multiplicatively (in error suppression).

This is additive composition: f(d1+d2)=f(d1)⋅f(d2)f(d_1 + d_2) = f(d_1) \cdot f(d_2). Theorem 1(2) gives exponential scaling: εd∝Λ−(d+1)/2\varepsilon_d \propto \Lambda^{-(d+1)/2}. The measured Λ=2.14±0.02\Lambda = 2.14 \pm 0.02 is the error suppression factor for each increase of two in code distance (Google Quantum AI and Collaborators 2024).

On this paper’s analogy, the composition operator would order quantum scaling above AI scaling: exponential functions eventually dominate any power law, and additive composition, where each step’s correction is independent of accumulated state, produces stronger scaling than multiplicative composition, where each step depends on (and is limited by) accumulated context. The ordering is this paper’s reading; Λ\Lambda is the source’s measured quantity, not an exponent of this framework.

5.3 Physics: bounded composition

In the time crystal, the source’s linear stability analysis gives a growing antisymmetric (breathing) mode for pairs in its active region; higher-order damping, which that analysis leaves out, can stabilise the growing mode, and the pair settles into steady-state oscillation on a linearly stable limit cycle (Morrell et al. 2026).

This is bounded composition, on this paper’s reading of the system: Qr+1=min⁡(Qr+δQr,Qmax)Q_{r+1} = \min(Q_r + \delta Q_r,\, Q_{\max}). The source records only the established oscillation, so no rise toward the cycle, no ceiling and no growth exponent has been measured (Section 1.1). On the framework’s reading, a recursive channel with intrinsic losses saturates; the time crystal is consistent with that reading and does not test it.

5.4 The phase diagram

The three composition types can be organised into a phase diagram with base quality (II, normalised) and coupling strength (βL\beta_L) as axes:
